title: Rate limits accrue continuously and are computed at call time, with Unlimited as a max-uint sentinel
content:
A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.2.2.1.3.1 gives the actual formula: `getCurrentRateLimit` returns `_min(d.slope * (block.timestamp - d.lastUpdated) + d.lastAmount, d.maxAmount)`, with a preceding special case — "Unlimited rate limit case: if `d.maxAmount == type(uint256).max`, return `type(uint256).max`."

Two implementation properties follow that the parameter tables alone do not reveal. First, replenishment is **lazy**: nothing refills the bucket on a schedule; available capacity is derived on read from the elapsed time since `lastUpdated`. There is no cron job, no keeper transaction, and no possibility of the refill mechanism failing independently of a call.

Second, `Unlimited` is not a very large number — it is a sentinel that bypasses the arithmetic entirely. Both `triggerRateLimitDecrease` and `triggerRateLimitIncrease` return early when `maxAmount == type(uint256).max`, so an unlimited key does no bookkeeping at all. `setUnlimitedRateLimitData` sets `maxAmount` and `lastAmount` to max-uint with `slope` 0 (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.2.2.1.3.3), which is coherent only because of the short-circuit — a slope of zero would otherwise mean capacity that never refills.

This clears up a reading puzzle in the parameter tables, where several limits appear as "maxAmount: Unlimited, slope: 0." That is not a one-time non-replenishing allowance; it is the canonical way of expressing "unmetered."
description: getCurrentRateLimit returns min(slope × elapsed + lastAmount, maxAmount), so capacity regenerates without any keeper — and maxAmount set to type(uint256).max short-circuits all accounting.
